407.title: Not by bread alone (Deuteronomy 8:1–3)
407.hook: the hunger in the wilderness taught them to live by every word
407.carry: carried, even when it didn't feel like it
407.howItsDone: Some Christians fast at certain times, such as Lent, Fridays or before communion, and Orthodox and Catholic Christians keep set fasting days; this verse is a common way to explain why.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ebed, and some of the hardest laws in the Bible. Your line was read the hard parts honestly. Today, a gentler page from the same book. Day four hundred seven.

Four in the afternoon, and lunch never happened. First a low hum in the stomach, then a tightness, then a short answer to someone who didn't deserve it. Hunger is honest. It shows, very fast, how much a body depends on things it usually doesn't think about. Now stretch that out to forty years of depending, morning after morning, on food that came with the dew and spoiled if it was saved. Moses is near the end of his life, and in Deuteronomy he's looking back at those years with the people. And he says something surprising about the hunger. It wasn't an accident. It was a lesson.
screen: `FOUR O'CLOCK, NO LUNCH.` → `HUNGER IS HONEST.` → `THE HUNGER WAS A LESSON.`

segments.voice: Moses says, in the King James Bible: "thou shalt remember all the way which the LORD thy God led thee these forty years in the wilderness." Remember the whole road. And then: "he humbled thee, and suffered thee to hunger, and fed thee with manna, which thou knewest not, neither did thy fathers know; that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD doth man live." Look at the order. First the hunger. Then the manna, a food nobody had ever seen, so nobody could take credit for it. And then the lesson: you need bread, yes, and you also need something bread can't give. You need the word that comes from God. Moses adds a tender detail in the very next verse: in all those forty years, your clothes didn't wear out, and your feet didn't swell. Carried, even when it didn't feel like it. Later, in the Gospels, Jesus is alone in the wilderness for forty days, fasting, and he's hungry. The tempter says: if you're the Son of God, turn these stones into bread. And Jesus answers with this verse from Deuteronomy, in slightly different words. In the King James Bible's version of Matthew: "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God." Christians who keep fasts, in Lent or before communion or at other times, often reach for this verse to explain them: not to punish the body, but to let a little hunger remind them what else they live on.
screen: `REMEMBER ALL THE WAY.` · `FIRST THE HUNGER, THEN THE MANNA.` · `CLOTHES THAT DIDN'T WEAR OUT.` · `JESUS ANSWERS WITH THIS VERSE.` · then, large: `MAN SHALL NOT LIVE BY BREAD ALONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go hungry a little, and listen. Only if it's safe for you: if you're pregnant, unwell, or have any history with food that makes this hard, skip the hunger and just do the listening. Otherwise, choose a small fast today: one snack, one coffee, one dessert you let go by. For now, settle and breathe, and notice what you're hungry for beyond food. Rest. Attention. Being known. A word from God. When the hunger comes later, let it be a bell that reminds you. If you pray, you can turn each pang into a short prayer. The bell holds the time.
Manna. The food nobody had seen before, given each morning in the wilderness, to teach that man does not live by bread alone.
Your line: carried, even when it didn't feel like it. Today, skip one small thing you'd normally eat or drink, and when you miss it, ask what else you're hungry for. Day four hundred seven.

408.title: Choose life (Deuteronomy 30:15–20)
408.hook: I set before you life and death: choose life
408.carry: near, in your mouth and in your heart
408.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Deuteronomy 30 when speaking about daily decisions and moral choices, and Paul quotes 'the word is nigh thee' from this chapter in Romans 10.

segments.voice: Yesterday, manna and the hunger that taught a lesson. Your line was carried, even when it didn't feel like it. What were you hungry for, besides food? Day four hundred eight.
screen: `CARRIED, EVEN WHEN IT DIDN'T FEEL LIKE IT.`

segments.voice: Plenty of the choices that shape a life don't feel like choices at all. They feel like Tuesday. Whether to text back or let it slide. Whether to go to bed or watch one more. Whether to say the true thing or the easy one. Whether to get up and walk or stay on the couch. Each one is tiny. But laid end to end, they become a direction. Moses is near the end of his great speech in Deuteronomy. He's spent chapters laying out the way of life he hopes his people will walk. And now he boils it all down to a single choice, and he sets it in front of them like two plates on a table.
screen: `CHOICES THAT FEEL LIKE TUESDAY.` → `END TO END, A DIRECTION.` → `TWO PLATES ON A TABLE.`

segments.voice: Here's how Moses says it, in the King James Bible: "See, I have set before thee this day life and good, and death and evil." And a few verses on, he calls witnesses: "I call heaven and earth to record this day against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live." Choose life. In Hebrew: u-vacharta ba-chayyim, and you shall choose life. Chayyim, life, is plural in form, and some readers hear in that plural that life is always more than one thing: breath and family and land and God, all at once. It's the same word in the Jewish toast, l'chaim, to life. Notice what Moses doesn't do. He doesn't choose for them. He sets it out, and he pleads. And just before this, he says something hopeful about how possible it is. This isn't too hard for you, he says, or far away. It isn't up in heaven, or across the sea. "But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it." The good life isn't a distant mountain to climb. It's as close as your own mouth. And then Moses says what life is: loving God, listening to his voice, holding on to him, "for he is thy life, and the length of thy days." Paul quotes the word is nigh thee in his letter to the Romans, and some Christian readers hear an echo of the two ways in Jesus' words about two roads, one narrow. And notice how often Moses says this day. The choice isn't saved for the end. It's on the table today.
screen: `LIFE AND GOOD, DEATH AND EVIL.` · `CHAYYIM: LIFE, ALWAYS PLURAL.` · `THE WORD IS VERY NIGH UNTO THEE.` · `FOR HE IS THY LIFE.` · then, large: `THEREFORE CHOOSE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose the life-giving option once. Settle, and breathe. Think ahead through the rest of your day. Somewhere in it there's a small fork: two plates on the table. One option leaves you, or someone else, a little more alive. Water instead of the third coffee. A walk instead of the scroll. Calling someone instead of putting it off. The kind answer instead of the clever one. Find that fork now, before it arrives. Picture yourself choosing life there. If you pray, you can ask for help to choose it. The bell holds the time.
Choose life. Moses' plea near the end of Deuteronomy: life and death are set before you, and the word is near, in your mouth and in your heart.
Your line: near, in your mouth and in your heart. Today, when you reach that small fork you found, pick the plate that gives life, and say the line to yourself as you do. Day four hundred eight.

409.title: Moses sees the land (Deuteronomy 34)
409.hook: on Mount Nebo he sees the land he'll never enter, and dies
409.howItsDone: Christian pilgrims visit Mount Nebo in Jordan, where a memorial church stands, and some preachers turn to Deuteronomy 34 at funerals and farewells to speak of work handed on to others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses set two plates before his people: life and death. Your line was near, in your mouth and in your heart. Where was your small fork, and which plate did you pick? Day four hundred nine.
screen: `NEAR, IN YOUR MOUTH AND IN YOUR HEART.`

segments.voice: An old man climbs a mountain. He's a hundred and twenty years old. Forty of those years he's spent walking a whole people through the desert: through complaints and manna, golden calves and giants, the long funeral march of a generation. And now they're camped by the Jordan River, one crossing away from the land they've been walking toward for forty years. But he won't cross. He's been told. So he climbs Mount Nebo, on the east side of the river, and at the top, God shows him everything: the hills to the north, the valleys, the palm-tree city of Jericho, all the way to the sea in the west.
screen: `A HUNDRED AND TWENTY YEARS OLD.` → `ONE RIVER AWAY.` → `UP NEBO, TO SEE.`

segments.voice: Then God says, in the King James Bible: "I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes, but thou shalt not go over thither." Why can't he go? Back in the book of Numbers, at a place called Meribah, Moses struck the rock twice with his rod instead of speaking to it as God told him, and he was told then that he wouldn't lead the people in. Readers still argue about whether that seems fair. The text doesn't argue. It just tells it. "So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab." And then a mysterious detail: he buried him, the text says, in a valley, and tradition reads he as God, "but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day." No grave to visit. No shrine. The man who led them out is gone, and the people go on without a monument. The chapter adds that "his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated." He didn't wear out. He was simply finished. And it ends with an epitaph: there arose not a prophet since in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face. Who wrote this chapter, describing Moses' own death? Jewish tradition in the Talmud offers more than one answer: some sages said Joshua wrote the last verses; others said Moses wrote them himself, in tears. Today Mount Nebo is in Jordan, and pilgrims climb it to look out over the same view. Moses gave his whole life to a promise he saw but didn't enter. Christians remember that he does appear, much later, on another mountain, talking with Jesus at the transfiguration.
screen: `SEE IT, BUT NOT GO OVER.` · `NO MAN KNOWETH HIS GRAVE.` · `HIS EYE WAS NOT DIM.` · `WHO WROTE HIS DEATH?` · then, large: `I HAVE CAUSED THEE TO SEE IT WITH THINE EYES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless a future you won't see. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're working toward that will likely outlast you, or that others will finish. Children or grandchildren. Students. A garden. A business, a church, a cause, a tree you planted. Picture it years from now, flourishing, without you in the picture. Notice what that feels like. Then, like Moses on the mountain, look out over it and let it be enough to have seen it begin. If you pray, you can bless it, and the people who'll carry it on. The bell holds the time.
Nebo. The mountain east of the Jordan where Moses, at a hundred twenty, saw the promised land he would never enter.
Your line: seeing is enough. Today, do one thing for someone who'll come after you, and don't wait to see how it turns out. Day four hundred nine.

410.title: Why Christians read the Torah
410.hook: Jesus quoted Deuteronomy in the desert and summed the law in two commandments from it
410.howItsDone: Most churches read from the Old Testament, including the Torah, in worship, and many Christians learn Jesus' summary of the law, the two great commandments, by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses on Mount Nebo, seeing the land he would never enter. Your line was seeing is enough. What did you do for someone who'll come after you? Day four hundred ten.

For five weeks now, this path has been walking through Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. Plagues and Passover. Manna and mountains. Corners of fields and cloaks given back by sundown. A fair question, on a Christian path: why? Most churches don't keep the food laws, and none offer animal sacrifices. So why read these books at all? Here's one place to start. When Jesus was alone in the desert, hungry and tempted three times, he answered three times. And every single answer was a quotation from one book. Deuteronomy.
screen: `FIVE WEEKS IN THE BOOKS OF MOSES.` → `A FAIR QUESTION: WHY?` → `THREE ANSWERS FROM ONE BOOK.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Torah is usually translated law, but it's closer to teaching, or instruction: the way a parent points a child down the right road. It's the Jewish name for the first five books of the Bible, the books of Moses. For Jesus, these were scripture. He grew up hearing them read in the synagogue. In the desert he answered the tempter with them: man shall not live by bread alone; thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God; worship God and serve him only. Then, near the end of his life, someone asks him which commandment is the greatest. He reaches into the Torah twice. In Matthew's Gospel, in the King James Bible: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets." The first comes from the Shema in Deuteronomy, the line right after hear, O Israel. The second is from Leviticus, the chapter with the corners of the field. Hang is a vivid word: like a door on its two hinges. Everything else swings on these two. And Jesus also said, "Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil." Christians have understood that in different ways. Catholic, Orthodox and many Protestant teachers distinguish the moral law, which still guides, from ceremonial laws they see as fulfilled in Christ. Lutherans often speak of law and gospel, the law showing our need and the gospel meeting it. But nearly all of them read these books as their own scripture, shared with the Jewish people, who read them first.
screen: `TORAH: TEACHING, NOT JUST LAW.` · `THREE ANSWERS FROM DEUTERONOMY.` · `TWO HINGES: GOD, AND NEIGHBOR.` · `NOT TO DESTROY, BUT TO FULFIL.` · then, large: `ON THESE TWO COMMANDMENTS HANG ALL THE LAW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read Matthew twenty-two, verses thirty-seven to forty. It's four verses. If you have a Bible or a phone nearby, find it after the bell, and read it slowly, twice. For now, settle and breathe, and hold the two hinges. On one breath, call the first hinge to mind: love God with all your heart and soul and mind. On the next, the second: love your neighbor as yourself. Back and forth, slowly, like a door swinging. Notice which one feels closer to your own life today. If you pray, you can ask for help with the harder one. The bell holds the time.
Torah. Hebrew for teaching or instruction, and the name for the five books of Moses that Jesus quoted and summed up in two commandments.
Your line: on these two hang all. Today, when you have a decision to make, ask the two-hinge question: is this love for God, and is this love for my neighbor? Day four hundred ten.

411.title: Block close: the wilderness road
411.hook: slaves, sea, manna, mountain, calf, and forty years of being carried
411.howItsDone: Some Christians describe hard seasons as 'wilderness' times, and Lent's forty days recall Jesus' forty days in the wilderness, which some readers link to Israel's forty years.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Torah, and Jesus hanging all the law on two commandments. Your line was on these two hang all. Did you ask the two-hinge question? Day four hundred eleven, and the close of the wilderness road.

Five weeks ago, this path opened on a people making bricks for a king who had forgotten them. Since then: two midwives who said no. A basket in the reeds. A bush on fire that didn't burn up, and a name, I AM. Ten plagues and a night of blood on the doorposts. A sea that opened. A tambourine. Bread on the ground every morning. Thunder on a mountain, ten words, a golden calf, and the back of God passing by. Corners of fields, a jubilee horn, twelve spies, a talking donkey, and an old man on Mount Nebo looking at a land he would never enter. Today we stand at the end of that road and look back.
screen: `BRICKS FOR A KING WHO FORGOT.` → `A SEA, A MOUNTAIN, A CALF.` → `TODAY WE LOOK BACK.`

segments.voice: The Hebrew name for the book of Numbers is Bemidbar: in the wilderness. And for these four books, that's where the people mostly are. Not in Egypt anymore. Not in the land yet. In between. It's a long, hard in-between. They complain, constantly. About the water, the food, Moses, the giants. They make a calf the moment Moses is late. A whole generation is too afraid to go in. If you read these books looking for heroes, you'll be disappointed by almost everyone, including, at Meribah, Moses himself. But read them again and notice who keeps showing up. Manna morning after morning, even on the mornings after they grumbled. Water from a rock. A pillar of cloud by day and fire by night. Clothes that didn't wear out. Here's how Moses sums it up in Deuteronomy, in the King James Bible: "in the wilderness, where thou hast seen how that the LORD thy God bare thee, as a man doth bear his son, in all the way that ye went, until ye came into this place." Bare thee: carried you. Like a father carrying a tired child on his shoulders the last mile home. That's the thread through the whole road. Not that the people were strong, or faithful, or patient. They mostly weren't. It's that they were carried. Christians read their own lives in this road too. Paul, writing to the church in Corinth, says these wilderness stories were written down as examples for later readers. Rescued from slavery, but not home yet; fed one day at a time; failing, and carried anyway. And tomorrow we open the songbook those carried people and their children would one day sing: the Psalms.
screen: `BEMIDBAR: IN THE WILDERNESS.` · `ALMOST NO HEROES.` · `MANNA, EVEN AFTER GRUMBLING.` · `CARRIED, AS A MAN BEARS HIS SON.` · then, large: `THE LORD THY GOD BARE THEE, AS A MAN DOTH BEAR HIS SON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your own wilderness season. Settle, and breathe. Think back to a stretch of your life that was in-between: out of one thing and not yet into the next. A move. A job lost. An illness. A breakup. A long wait. Name it, simply. Then look for the manna. What kept showing up, day by day, even when you were grumbling? A friend. A routine. A small mercy. Someone's casserole. Notice that you came through. If you pray, you can thank God for carrying you. If not, thank whoever did. The bell holds the time.
Bemidbar. Hebrew for in the wilderness, the name of the book of Numbers: the long in-between where Israel was carried, not strong, from slavery to the edge of the land.
Your line: carried through the desert. Today, tell one person about a hard season you came through, and who carried you. Day four hundred eleven.

412.title: The tree by the water (Psalm 1)
412.hook: the happy person is like a tree planted by rivers
412.howItsDone: Christians pray the Psalms in the Liturgy of the Hours, in the Anglican Daily Office and in personal devotions; some monastic communities pray the whole Psalter each week.

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the wilderness road, bemidbar, from slavery to the edge of the land. Your line was carried through the desert. What season of your own were you carried through? Day four hundred twelve, and a new block begins.

Today we open a different kind of book. Not a story this time. A songbook. A hundred and fifty poems: praise and complaint, thanks and rage, songs for a crowd and songs for one person awake at night. Monks chant them in the dark before dawn. People whisper them at bedsides. The Psalms. For the next fifty days, this path reads the Psalms and the wisdom books, a psalm a day to start. And the very first psalm, the front door to the whole collection, doesn't open with a command or a story. It opens with a picture. A tree, growing beside a stream.
screen: `A NEW BLOCK: THE PSALMS.` → `A HUNDRED AND FIFTY SONGS.` → `THE FRONT DOOR IS A TREE.`

segments.voice: Psalm one begins, in the King James Bible: "Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful." Notice the slow drift. Walking. Then standing. Then sitting. First you're just passing by bad advice, then you stop and linger, then you've pulled up a chair and become a scoffer yourself. Nobody sits down all at once. Blessed here is the Hebrew ashrei, which also means happy, or how fortunate. The book of praises opens with: oh, the happiness of. Then: "But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night." Meditate, in Hebrew hagah, is a sound word. It's used elsewhere for a dove's moan and a lion's growl over its prey. To meditate on scripture was to murmur it under your breath, over and over, chewing on it. And then the picture: "And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither." In a dry land, a tree beside an irrigation channel is a small miracle. Its roots go down to water nobody sees. It still has seasons. It doesn't fruit all year. But it doesn't dry up in the heat. The psalm ends with the other kind of life, which it calls chaff, the husks that blow away on the threshing floor. Two ways, the last verse says: the way of the righteous, and the way of the ungodly. Right at the door of the book. Saint Benedict's Rule for monks spreads all hundred and fifty psalms across each week, and some communities still keep that weekly round.
screen: `WALK, STAND, SIT: THE SLOW DRIFT.` · `ASHREI: OH, THE HAPPINESS.` · `HAGAH: MURMUR IT, LIKE A DOVE.` · `ROOTS DOWN TO HIDDEN WATER.` · then, large: `LIKE A TREE PLANTED BY THE RIVERS OF WATER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit by water or a tree. If you can, go to one now, or just to a window where you can see one. If you can't, picture one: a tree you know, beside a creek or a canal or a fountain. Settle, and breathe. Imagine its roots spreading underground, reaching down toward water you can't see. Then murmur one line under your breath, the old way, again and again: planted by the water. If you pray, you can ask where your roots are reaching. The bell holds the time.
Ashrei. Hebrew for blessed, happy, how fortunate, the first word of the Psalms: the life rooted like a tree by hidden water, fruit in its season.
Your line: planted by the water. Today, notice what you drift toward, walking, standing, sitting, and give five minutes to whatever waters your roots. Day four hundred twelve.

what it means: a picture at the door of the Psalms: a life rooted in hidden water, with seasons, that doesn't wither in the heat.

413.title: What is man? (Psalm 8)
413.hook: the moon and stars, and yet God is mindful of us
413.carry: what are we, that you care?
413.howItsDone: Christians pray Psalm 8 in daily prayer and at services that give thanks for creation, and the letter to the Hebrews (chapter 2) reads it as pointing to Jesus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first psalm, ashrei: a tree with its roots in hidden water. Your line was planted by the water. What watered your roots? Day four hundred thirteen, the end of week fifty-nine.

Go outside on a clear night, away from the streetlights, and look up long enough for your eyes to adjust. At first a few stars. Then dozens. Then a haze of them, too many to count, and maybe the pale smear of the Milky Way. Out there, it's easy to feel two things at once. Very small. And, strangely, more awake than all week. Long ago, someone stood under that same sky, with no telescopes and no streetlights, and the psalm's heading names him David. He wrote down a question people are still asking.
screen: `A CLEAR NIGHT, NO STREETLIGHTS.` → `VERY SMALL, AND VERY AWAKE.` → `THE SAME SKY, LONG AGO.`

segments.voice: Psalm eight opens and closes with the same line, in the King James Bible: "O LORD our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth!" Praise as bookends. And in between, the question: "When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained; What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?" Notice the work of thy fingers. Not God's arm, not his mighty hand. Fingers, like someone doing fine embroidery. The whole night sky is fingerwork. Next to that, what are we? A breath. A speck. And yet God is mindful of us, remembers us, comes to see us. Then the psalm turns the other way: "For thou hast made him a little lower than the angels, and hast crowned him with glory and honour." The Hebrew word there is elohim, which can mean God or heavenly beings. The King James says angels, and so does the letter to the Hebrews when it quotes this verse; some translations say a little lower than God. Small, and crowned. And given dominion, the psalm says, over the sheep and oxen, the birds and the fish. Some readers hear in that a charge to care for the world, not only to rule it. The New Testament letter to the Hebrews quotes these verses and hears them fulfilled in Jesus, crowned with glory after being made low. And what a week it's been: manna, choose life, Moses on Nebo, the Torah, the wilderness road, a tree by the water, and now the stars.
screen: `THE WORK OF THY FINGERS.` · `WHAT IS MAN, THAT THOU ART MINDFUL?` · `SMALL, AND CROWNED.` · `SMALL, YET GIVEN DOMINION.` · then, large: `O LORD OUR LORD, HOW EXCELLENT IS THY NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look up at the sky. If you can, step outside or go to a window now. If it's daytime, look at the clouds or the blue and remember the stars are still there behind it. Settle, and breathe. Let yourself feel small. Really small: one person on one planet, circling one star among more than anyone can count. Then let the second half of the psalm in: and yet, remembered. And yet, cared for. Hold both, small and crowned, together. If you pray, you can ask the psalm's question out loud: what am I, that you care? The bell holds the time.
What is man? The psalmist's question under the night sky: so small next to the moon and stars, and yet remembered, and crowned with glory.

Your line: what are we, that you care? Tonight, look up for one minute before bed. And that's week fifty-nine: bread, life, Nebo, the Torah, the wilderness road, a tree, and the stars. Day four hundred thirteen.

fork.setup: you're lying under the night sky, the moon and stars all around. the psalmist asks, what is man? what's the psalm's answer?
options: small, and yet remembered and crowned.
fork.reveal: both at once: so small God need not notice, and yet God is mindful of us, and crowns us with glory and honor.

original.note: Hebrew: what is man? Enosh is one of the Hebrew words for a human being.

trapdoor: what you thought: humans are tiny and don't matter.
what it means: tiny under the stars, and yet remembered, visited, crowned, and given dominion.
what a scholar hears: elohim, 'God' or 'heavenly beings', rendered angels by the KJV and by Hebrews 2:7, which reads the psalm of Jesus.
